nameStory: The red-stalked evening primrose gets its name from two key features: the reddish coloration on its stems and its family connection to evening primroses, which traditionally open their flowers in the evening hours. While not all evening primroses strictly follow this evening-blooming pattern, the name stuck as these plants became known for their late-day flower displays that attract night-flying moths.
description: Red-stalked evening primrose is a wildflower in the evening primrose family, distinguished primarily by its reddish-tinted stems. Like other evening primroses, it produces four-petaled yellow flowers and grows as an upright plant. This species is quite rare in New England, making it an exciting find for plant enthusiasts. It typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a branching structure.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - stems have a noticeable reddish or purplish tint, feeling smooth to slightly rough when you run your finger along them

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with four broad petals that feel delicate and papery, typically opening in late afternoon or evening with a faint, sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately along the stem, with a slightly fuzzy texture and edges that may have small teeth

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright branching plant reaching 1-3 feet tall, often forming small colonies in favorable spots

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing small seeds that feel almost dust-like between your fingers

habitat: Red-stalked evening primrose prefers disturbed soils and open areas such as roadsides, field edges, and sandy or gravelly sites. In New England, look for it in well-drained locations with full sun exposure. Given its rarity in the region, it's most likely to be found in southern New England areas with suitable habitat.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with characteristic reddish stems becoming apparent as the plant develops its branching structure.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with yellow flowers opening in late afternoon and evening, best viewed from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, releasing seeds while the reddish stem coloration often intensifies.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving dried stems that may persist and still show traces of the red coloration.

funFact: This evening primrose is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only three times by naturalists - making it one of the most elusive wildflowers in the region and a true treasure for anyone lucky enough to find it!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with common evening primrose, but the red-stalked variety's distinctly reddish or purplish stems set it apart from the green stems of its common cousin. Remember: "Red stems, rare stems" - if you see reddish coloring on the stalks, you've likely found something special.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "evening" primrose, these plants aren't related to true primroses at all - they're in a completely different plant family. The evening primrose family includes many species that bloom at different times of day, so don't expect them all to follow the evening schedule suggested by their name.
compareHints: Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems. The flower structure and general plant form are quite similar across the genus, making the stem color the key distinguishing feature. Yellow sundrops and small sundrops tend to be shorter with different growth patterns, while the various other evening primroses lack the distinctive red stem coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers.
Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose.
Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening.
Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species.
Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
